fullName: 3D Micro & Nano Diffraction — polychromatic (Laue) and monochromatic micro/nano-diffraction with depth resolution

status2026.detail: APS weekly 'Beamline Commissioning Progress' chart dated 2026-10-05 lists '34-ID-E: 3DMN XSD' at stage 5 of 6 ('Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments'), not yet stage 6 ('Restart of General User Program'). The APS Proposal Types page (updated 2026-10-07) already lists 34-ID-E among beamlines taking General User and Rapid Access proposals. History: Jan 2025 update said 3DMN/ATOMIC infrastructure would be 'in construction' after the other seven feature beamlines; Aug 2025 update put 3DMN in technical commissioning with first experiments expected early 2026; the Jan 26 2026 chart still showed stage 4 (technical commissioning). The APS-U project itself received final DOE approval (CD-4) in Jan 2026. A talk at the ModSim 2026 workshop (BNL, 12–14 Aug 2026) by the APS coded-aperture team reported that the beamline had been down since mid-2023, that early 2D experiments had run about two weeks before the talk (i.e. around late July 2026), that HPC-scale (3D, coded-aperture) experiments would start in winter, and that 34-ID-E is planning a new detector with ≈10× faster collection.

tagline: A 'rainbow' X-ray beam as fine as a virus maps, in 3D, how the tiny crystals inside a material are tilted and stretched.
summary: Metals, rocks and microchips are made of tiny crystals, or grains; how each grain is tilted, squeezed and stretched decides whether a turbine blade cracks or a transistor works. At 34-ID-E, 3D Micro & Nano Diffraction (3DMN) maps that in 3D. Mirrors focus a 'rainbow' beam, X-rays of many energies at once (roughly 5–30 keV), into a spot designed to be about 100 nm wide; a second station aims for 40 nm. Each grain the beam crosses reflects the energies that fit its atomic layers, throwing a Laue pattern of spots onto a camera half a metre above; the pattern reveals the grain's orientation and distortion. A platinum wire or tiny gold barcode sweeps just above the surface; the spots it hides show how deep each signal came from. As of October 2026, 3DMN is in scientific commissioning: early experiments began in summer, and it already takes general-user proposals.

whatAPSUEnables.text: A focusing mirror forms a shrunken image of the X-ray source, so a smaller source allows a smaller spot. In the design's brightness mode, the upgraded ring's electron source is about 19 times narrower horizontally (14.7 µm root-mean-square width instead of 280 µm) and 3 times narrower vertically, and more precisely shaped mirrors can use the whole beam: the old ones reached about 500 nm only when stopped down to a 60 µm opening. The design spots shrink from 300–500 nm to about 100 nm and 40 nm, fine enough to resolve strain inside the walls of tangled defects that harden metals. A more coherent beam also makes lens-free 3D imaging of single grains practical. The design team multiplied a brighter source (×100), better mirrors (×9), coded-aperture depth scans (×5) and low-noise detectors (×10): about 900 times faster for most experiments and up to 45,000 times for some. These are design estimates; the detector purchases were cut from the project, and no as-built spot size is published.
quantitative: Horizontal electron source size: 280 µm rms before the upgrade → 14.7 µm rms (APS-U brightness mode, 324 bunches); vertical 10 → 3.2 µm rms.

Source brightness rises by a factor of ≈100, and the FDR says focused spot size and intensity improve 'linearly with the brightness'. Caveat: this is loose wording. For fixed optics, focused flux density scales with source brightness, while spot size scales with source size × demagnification, not linearly with brightness. FDR Chapter 1 quotes a larger brightness gain (≈540× at 20 keV for an undulator optimized for 20 keV, Table 1.1); '≈100' is the 3DMN section's round number.

Focus: 300 × 300 nm (pre-upgrade web specification) or 300–500 nm (H) × 300–700 nm (V) (wiki) → design 103 × 68 nm² (micro) and 37 × 37 nm² (nano) at 14 keV. These are FWHM-like sizes; the RMS sizes are ≈50 × 35 and ≈19 × 19 nm.
Pink-beam flux on the sample: ≈10¹¹ ph/s before the upgrade → ≈10¹⁴ ph/s design; monochromatic ≈10⁹ → ≈10¹¹ (directory) to ≈10¹² (PDR) ph/s.
The old KB mirrors reached ≈500 nm only when apertured to ≈60 × 60 µm²; fully illuminated new mirrors give ≈9× more flux at the same or a smaller spot.
PDR overall gain estimate: ≈900× for most experiments, ≈4,500× for many and up to ≈45,000× for some.

Depth scans: a coded aperture needs ≈120 µm of scan (8 bits × 15 µm) vs a 600 µm wire scan in 1 µm steps, ≈5× fewer frames with lower noise; the PDR target is 400 instead of 2,000 images per depth scan.
Projected raw data: ≈2.8 PB a year, vs ≈400 TB a year at pre-upgrade 34-ID-E.

Estimated horizontal coherent fraction at 14 keV: ≈0.2% before the upgrade → ≈9% with APS-U, using Gaussian source sizes and divergences from FDR Table 1.1 plus single-electron undulator terms for a 2.1 m device (derived here; approximate).

techniques.name: Polychromatic (pink-beam) Laue micro/nano-diffraction
techniques.text: Polychromatic Laue diffraction shines a beam of many X-ray energies at once, a 'pink' beam (the mirror has trimmed the highest energies from the undulator's spectrum), at a sample that stays still. Each set of atomic layers in a grain reflects the wavelength that fits its spacing and angle (Bragg's law), so every grain throws a pattern of spots whose directions fingerprint how it is oriented and how its shape is distorted. A spot reveals its direction but not its wavelength, so the pattern gives the deviatoric strain, the five components of distortion that change shape, but not the overall swelling or shrinking; typical precision is about 10⁻⁴, at best about 2 × 10⁻⁵. Scanning the sample gives 2D maps, and depth resolution adds the third dimension. Most of the useful signal on the top detector comes from 12–17 keV X-rays.

techniques.name: Differential-aperture X-ray microscopy (wire scan)
techniques.text: Differential-aperture X-ray microscopy (DAXM) adds depth to Laue diffraction. The beam passes deep into the sample, so spots made at many depths land on the detector together. A platinum wire, about 50–100 µm thick, is stepped about 1 µm at a time within a millimetre of the surface; when its edge hides a spot in one frame but not the previous one, the straight line from that detector pixel past the wire's edge meets the incoming beam at the depth where the spot was made. Typical resolution is 0.5–1 µm along the beam. The method was introduced at the APS by an Oak Ridge team (Larson, Yang, Ice, Budai and Tischler, Nature 2002) and became the signature technique of 34-ID-E.

techniques.name: Coded-aperture depth-resolved Laue (mask scan)
techniques.text: Coded-aperture Laue replaces the wire with a gold 'barcode' that slides over the diffracted beams. Its 256-bit pattern of gold bars and gaps follows a de Bruijn sequence, in which every run of 8 bits appears only once, so the on-off pattern each spot traces as the mask moves identifies where along the mask it was seen, and from that the depth it came from. About 120 µm of scan (8 bits of 15 µm) is enough, against about 600 µm for a wire, so a depth scan needs about five times fewer frames and has less noise; software decodes it with a search followed by a least-squares fit. Demonstrated at 34-ID-E before the upgrade and published in 2022–2025, it is expected to become the default once the reconstruction software matures.

techniques.name: Monochromatic energy-scan micro/nano-diffraction
techniques.text: With the monochromator in, the beam has a single energy, selected to about one part in 10,000 by two silicon crystals. Scanning that energy until an indexed Laue spot lights up measures its exact wavelength, and so the true spacing of those atomic layers: the one quantity a multi-energy pattern cannot give. That fixes the overall scale of the lattice and completes the strain measurement, all six components including the overall swelling or shrinking; combined with the wire, energy scans give depth-resolved lattice spacings. One cost: the monochromator reflects sideways, the plane in which horizontally polarized X-rays reflect least efficiently, so flux losses grow toward low energies, by estimates from about 5–10% at 12 keV to between a quarter and a half at 5.3 keV.

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffraction imaging on Laue-indexed grains
techniques.text: Bragg coherent diffraction imaging turns the speckled fringe around one diffraction spot into a 3D image of a single grain, showing its shape and the strain inside it. 3DMN pairs it with Laue diffraction: the multi-energy pattern first reveals exactly how a grain is oriented, so the energy that brings a chosen reflection onto a detector can be predicted. Then a single-energy beam is used, a movable detector about 2–3 m away records the speckle, and energy scans take the place of rotating the sample. The upgraded source's coherence, its waves in step across the beam, makes this practical; the design offers it at the micro station only.

techniques.name: Scanning X-ray fluorescence
techniques.text: Atoms struck by the beam emit X-rays at energies characteristic of each element (X-ray fluorescence), so a detector beside the sample maps which elements are where. At 3DMN this mainly helps locate features and landmarks before a diffraction map. The detector is an energy-dispersive silicon drift detector of the Vortex class; the preliminary design preferred a 1 mm thick sensor to catch higher-energy emission lines.

scienceCases.title: Hidden stresses inside dislocation cells of deformed metals
scienceCases.text: When copper is bent, its dislocations, line defects in the stacking of atoms, tangle into walls that divide each grain into cells. Depth-resolved Laue microscopy at the APS (Levine and colleagues, 2006) measured the elastic strain cell by cell and found it surprisingly large and widely spread; follow-up work found walls and cell interiors strained in opposite directions, as Mughrabi's composite model predicts. 3DMN aims for voxels, 3D pixels, of about 100 nm to resolve strain inside a single wall. A 2026 study fed pre-upgrade 34-ID-E wire scans of one grain of stainless steel, stretched by 2% and mapped with 0.5 µm depth resolution, to an unsupervised machine-learning model that picked out the cell structure and its strain.

scienceCases.title: The strain field of a single dislocation
scienceCases.text: A dislocation is a single line defect in the stacking of atoms, but it bends the crystal around it. Hofmann and colleagues (2013) mapped the rotations and strains around one dislocation at 34-ID-E, in a thin freestanding membrane of gallium arsenide and indium gallium arsenide (GaAs/In₀.₂Ga₀.₈As/GaAs), and found them matching elasticity theory that allows for the crystal's direction-dependent stiffness. Doing the same for a dislocation buried in bulk material needs beams smaller than 100 nm, one of the stated reasons for building 3DMN.

scienceCases.title: Additively manufactured (3D-printed) alloys
scienceCases.text: Metal 3D printing freezes molten alloy into tree-like dendrites, with the chemistry changing every few hundred nanometres. In nickel superalloys of the IN625 and IN718 type, the main dendrite arms are about 1 µm apart and the side arms about 300 nm, with matching segregation of alloying elements, so strain measurements at 34-ID-E before the upgrade averaged over the structure. A probe below 200 nm, combined with energy scans, is designed to measure the complete strain, all six components, at that scale.

scienceCases.title: Materials at terapascal pressure
scienceCases.text: Squeezing materials such as hydrogen between diamond tips to millions of atmospheres leaves samples only a few micrometres wide, and nano-fabricated anvil tips shrink them toward 100 nm. The science case cites the crystal structures of hydrogen phases III–V (samples 1–3 µm across) and diffraction at terapascal pressures, about 10 million atmospheres, as needing beams of about 50 nm with about 100 times more brightness. The micro station's long working distance was chosen to leave room for such cells.

scienceCases.title: Strain engineering in transistors and oxide devices
scienceCases.text: Chip makers deliberately stretch silicon so that electrons move through it faster. 3DMN aims to map that strain inside finished devices, including strain gradients at edges and interfaces in silicon-on-insulator and CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) structures with features below 32 nm. It also aims to watch nanoscale domains (stripes, toroids and bubbles) switch under applied fields and changing temperature in ferroelectrics, whose built-in electric polarization can be flipped, and multiferroics, which combine that with magnetism. The preliminary design report quotes IBM on industry's need for smaller probes.

scienceCases.title: Find a grain, then image it coherently
scienceCases.text: In a material made of many grains, you first need to know which grain to look at and how it is turned. The Laue pattern provides that map; then a single-energy coherent beam can image a chosen grain, or a small particle of another phase (a precipitate) inside it, in 3D. The design case: work out the grain orientations in the superalloy Inconel 617 with the multi-energy beam, predict the energy and direction of a reflection from a carbide precipitate at a triple junction, where three grains meet, and record it coherently on a detector 2–3 m away. Similar Laue-then-coherent-imaging work was shown in 2020 at 34-ID-C, and on tungsten samples cut out with a focused ion beam to contain chosen dislocations.

scienceCases.title: Coded apertures for fast 3D Laue
scienceCases.text: Borrowing an idea from X-ray astronomy, an APS team replaced the depth-finding wire with a gold barcode so that 3D scans need far fewer frames. In a test before the upgrade on a 75 µm nickel foil, with a 7–30 keV multi-energy beam focused to about 300 nm and the detector 510.9 mm above, the coded aperture recovered the full depth range of about 100 µm with less noise than a 100 µm platinum wire, using five times fewer scan points. Follow-up work added digital autofocusing, which calibrates the mask's exact position, and design rules: bits at least as large as the signal, an aspect ratio near 1, and scans of at least 8 bits.

keyParameters.label: Energy range
keyParameters.note: FDR beam-delivery spec (shared with ATOMIC). Current APS Beamline Directory lists 5.5–30 keV; pre-upgrade 34-ID-E was 7–30 keV. Upper limit set by mirror critical angle; lower by mono geometry.

keyParameters.label: Source
keyParameters.value: Planar hybrid PM undulator, 28 mm period, 2.1 m, upstream slot of canted straight (outboard branch)
keyParameters.note: FDR Table 4.62. Max power 777 W through 2 × 2 mm² FE mask at 30 m with K = 2.459. As-built era: IPAC'24 (Dejus et al.) lists the new 2.8 cm canted HPMUs with required K = 2.48 at 8.5 mm minimum gap, E1 = 3.0 keV, canted length ≈2.1 m.

keyParameters.label: Canting
keyParameters.value: 1 mrad between 3DMN (outboard/upstream) and ATOMIC (inboard/downstream)
keyParameters.note: 0.5 mrad canting magnets at both ends + 1 mrad magnet between the two undulators.

keyParameters.label: Front end
keyParameters.value: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE), windowless (differential pump), 2 × (2 mm H × 2 mm V) exit apertures 1 mrad apart at 25.4 m; 2 × 10 kW
keyParameters.note: Exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.

keyParameters.label: First mirror (34ID-MR-1)
keyParameters.value: Flat, horizontally deflecting, 3.0 mrad, Si/Rh/Pt stripes, notched substrate, at 29.6 m
keyParameters.note: Absorbs up to ≈189 W (Si stripe, 1 × 1 mm² acceptance, 9.1 keV 3rd harmonic), 0.48 W/mm² (FDR Table 4.66). PDR (2017) had proposed LN₂-cooled Si mirrors. Deflection sense: FDR text does not state it, but the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic (angles exaggerated) shows the 3DMN mirror steering its beam further outboard and the ATOMIC mirror steering inboard, as the PDR proposed.

keyParameters.label: Monochromator (34ID-MN-2)
keyParameters.value: Horizontally deflecting Si(111) double-crystal, ≈1.1 mm offset, pink-beam bypass, heated 2nd crystal (ΔT ≈ 60 K), at 53.8 m
keyParameters.note: Si(111) inferred from FDR Table 4.67 (12.5° at 9.1 keV) and stated in PDR. Acceptance needed < 300 × 300 µm². Pre-upgrade precursor: a new 1 mm-offset, horizontally reflecting Si(111) 'synthetic channel-cut' (6–20 keV, air-bearing granite stage, chamber slid sideways to switch pink/mono, heated 2nd crystal) was installed at 34-ID-C before the upgrade (Pateras et al. 2020).

keyParameters.label: Energy resolution (mono)
keyParameters.value: dE/E ≈ 10⁻⁴
keyParameters.note: Si(111) double bounce; same as pre-upgrade spec.

keyParameters.label: Micro-focus spot (design, 14 keV)
keyParameters.value: 103 × 68 nm² (H × V) brightness mode; 91 × 100 nm² timing mode
keyParameters.note: ShadowOui ray trace, FDR Table 4.64; KB at ≈60 m. Current Beamline Directory quotes 0.15 × 0.15 µm. No published as-built measurement found. Size definition is not stated in Table 4.64; the same ray traces give RMS ≈50 (H) × 35 (V) nm at zero figure error (FDR Fig. 4.61), so the tabulated values are ≈2× RMS, i.e. FWHM-like. APS-U Key Performance Parameters for feature beamlines were brightness at a defined energy plus usable energy range (only ISN had a focal-spot KPP), so 'all feature beamlines met their KPPs' (MEDSI 2025) does not certify a 3DMN spot size.

keyParameters.label: Nano-focus spot (design, 14 keV)
keyParameters.value: 37 × 37 nm² brightness mode; 38 × 37 nm² timing mode
keyParameters.note: KB at ≈65.5 m. Whether the nano station is installed/commissioned as of Oct 2026 is not documented publicly. RMS ≈19 × 19 nm in the same ray traces (FDR Fig. 4.61).

keyParameters.label: Flux on sample (design)
keyParameters.value: Micro 4.9 × 10¹², nano 4.9 × 10¹¹ ph/s/0.1%BW at 14 keV; pink ≈10¹⁴ ph/s; mono ≈10¹¹–10¹² ph/s
keyParameters.note: Pink/mono totals from PDR and Beamline Directory (10¹⁴ pink; 10¹¹ mono at 15 keV).

keyParameters.label: KB mirrors
keyParameters.value: Two fixed-figure (prefigured elliptical cylinder) Pt-coated KB pairs at 3.0 mrad; micro at ≈60 m, nano at ≈65.5 m
keyParameters.note: Figure-error tolerance (<10% spot growth): micro H 0.75 nm, V 0.5 nm rms; nano H 0.5 nm, V 0.4 nm rms.

keyParameters.label: Working distance
keyParameters.value: ≥ 50 mm (micro, design goal); ≈30 mm (nano)
keyParameters.note: PDR 2017 values; PDR also gives focal lengths f_h = 70 mm, f_v = 142 mm (62 m station) and 55/120 mm (66 m station) – may differ as built.

keyParameters.label: Detector geometry (reference: pre-upgrade 34-ID-E)
keyParameters.value: PerkinElmer XRD1621 (2048 × 2048, 200 µm pixels, 409.6 mm square) ≈511–513 mm above sample in 90° reflection geometry; two 1024 × 1024 (204.8 mm) PE side panels ≈0.40 m perpendicular distance (≈0.43 m to panel centre), outboard and inboard
keyParameters.note: From Gursoy et al. 2022 (510.9 mm), Das et al. 2018 ('XRD 1621', ≈511 mm) and lauelab geometry files geoN_2022-03-29 / 2023-04-06 (top 'PE1621 723-3335', P_z ≈513 mm; sides 'PE0822 883-4841/4843', P_z ≈400 mm, |P| ≈428 mm). Model naming is inconsistent across APS sources: the 2024 computing strategy lists 'PE XRD 1620 AN' + '2 × PE XRD 0820 AN', the 34-ID-E Instruments page lists XRD 0820 AN, while the 2022–23 geometry files identify the side panels as PE0822 units. 3DMN design calls for Pilatus-6M-class top detector + two 1–2M side detectors (computing strategy: Pilatus 6M + 2 × 2 MP, 6 → 10 Mpixel per point), but detector purchases were descoped from APS-U; as-built detectors unknown. A ModSim 2026 talk (Aug 2026) says 34-ID-E is planning a new detector with ≈10× collection speed (model not stated; the same slides mention wire reconstructions 'with Eiger').

keyParameters.label: Sample geometry
keyParameters.value: Sample surface inclined 45° to the incident beam; wire moves along H = (Y+Z)/√2
keyParameters.note: 34-ID-E coordinates: X horizontal outboard, Y up, Z along beam; 45° reflection geometry.

keyParameters.label: Depth-resolving aperture
keyParameters.value: Pt wire (≈50 µm historically; 100 µm in 2022 tests; 101.5 µm in geometry files) ≈0.2–1 mm above sample; or Au coded aperture (4.6 µm Au, 7.5/15 µm bits, 256-bit de Bruijn)
keyParameters.note: ≈50 µm Pt wire ≈200 µm above surface on the 34-ID-E 'End near focus' photo page (CCD-era, pre-2009 setup); ≈50 µm wire.

keyParameters.label: Depth resolution
keyParameters.value: ≈0.5–1 µm along the beam (DAXM, pre-upgrade)
keyParameters.note: 0.5 µm in SharafEldin et al. 2026; 1 µm steps in coded-aperture work. Goal ≈100 nm with the new beams, at ≈5× more frames per scan unless coded apertures are used.

keyParameters.label: Strain resolution
keyParameters.value: ≈10⁻⁴ in deviatoric strain (best ≈2 × 10⁻⁵)
keyParameters.note: PDR: 'dd/d = 10⁻⁴'; 1999 APS report: better than 2 parts in 10⁵ under favourable conditions. Deviatoric tensor from white-beam indexing (Chung & Ice 1999); complete tensor by adding one monochromatic energy measurement (Ice et al. 2005). Geometry check (derived here): one 200 µm pixel at ≈511 mm is ≈3.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad in 2θ, i.e. ≈2 × 10⁻⁴ in plane-normal direction / dd/d at 2θ = 90°, so the ≈10⁻⁴ (best ≈2 × 10⁻⁵) figures rely on sub-pixel peak fitting over many reflections (the PDR's '1 pixel ≈ 10⁻⁴' design rule would need ≈1 m detector distance).

keyParameters.label: Thermal stability requirement
keyParameters.value: Hutch 0.03–0.05 °C; nano-instrument enclosure ≤ 0.02 °C
keyParameters.note: A 100 mm Al part grows 100 nm for a 0.04 °C change (PDR).

keyParameters.label: Distances
keyParameters.value: Micro instrument 60.0 m, nano instrument 65.5 m, pink beam stop 66.9 m from source
keyParameters.note: FDR Table 4.63.

keyParameters.label: Analysis software
keyParameters.value: LaueGo (Igor Pro; wire-scan reconstruction, peak search, indexing 'euler', strain refinement) → lauelab (Python/C/CUDA, alpha, 2023-) and laue-portal (Dash web workflow, HPC/Polaris)
keyParameters.note: LaueGo by J. Z. Tischler; lauelab reproduces LaueGo arithmetic and supports wire-scan reconstruction and indexing; laue-portal; coded-aperture decoder 'cold'; 50 Polaris nodes processed 6–12 h coded-aperture scans (data from Feb/Apr 2023) and returned results 12–15 min behind the detector (SC'23 Workshops / XLOOP 2023 best paper). Background: Liu & Ice 2014 chapter.

insertionDevices.name: 3DMN undulator (U28, upstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (new APS-U structure: NdFeB with heavy-rare-earth grain-boundary-diffusion coercivity enhancement, vanadium-permendur poles)
insertionDevices.notes: Upstream device of the canted 34-ID straight → outboard branch. K up to ≈2.46 (value used for FDR max-power calc: 777 W through 2 × 2 mm² at 30 m); IPAC'24 lists required K = 2.48 at the 8.5 mm minimum gap, E1 = 3.0 keV. First harmonic E1 = 12.2/(1+K²/2) keV at 6 GeV → ≈3.0 keV at K=2.459 (3rd harmonic 9.1 keV, FDR Table 4.66); higher energies via odd harmonics. APS-U HPMU drive: min gap 8.5 mm, gap taper up to 5 mm (useful to broaden the pink spectrum for Laue, as requested in the PDR). Note: ATOMIC's directory entry quotes 2.3 m for its revolver; the FDR value (2.1 m) is used here and is supported by IPAC'24 ('canted length ≈2.1 m, full length ≈2.4 m').

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC undulator (revolver U25/U21, downstream) – partner beamline
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid PM revolver undulator (two magnet arrays, 25 and 21 mm)
insertionDevices.notes: Downstream device → inboard branch feeding ATOMIC (34-ID-F). Max power 763/738 W through 2 × 2 mm² at 30 m (K = 1.939/1.305). Not part of 3DMN but shares the straight, canting magnets and front end.

source.canting: Two undulators canted by 1.0 mrad (0.5 mrad magnets at each end of the straight and a 1 mrad magnet between the devices). 3DMN = upstream device = outboard beam; ATOMIC = downstream device = inboard beam. Before the upgrade (after the 2011 canting upgrade) the assignment was reversed: 34-ID-E took the inboard (downstream) beam and 34-ID-C the outboard beam.
source.frontEnd: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE) rated 2 × 10 kW and 280 kW/mrad², windowless exit with differential pumping, clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, burn-through fixed mask, GRID fluorescence XBPM1 (+ XBPM2 integrated in the exit mask), photon and safety shutters; exit mask at 25.4 m with two 2 × 2 mm² apertures 1 mrad apart; W exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: APS-U electron beam at the ID (FDR Table 1.1), brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm): σx = 14.7 µm, σy = 3.2 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy' = 1.3 µrad; timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm): 12.9 / 8.8 µm, 2.5 / 3.7 µrad. Pre-upgrade APS: 280 / 10 µm, 11.6 / 3.4 µrad. Single-electron photon terms for a 2.1 m device at 14 keV (derived here, σr = √(2·λ·L)/(4·π), σr' = √(λ/(2L))): ≈1.5 µm and ≈4.6 µrad, giving total photon source ≈14.8 × 3.6 µm rms and ≈5.4 × 4.8 µrad rms. Caveat: the canted source points sit ≈1 m either side of the straight centre where beta functions differ slightly.

branches.name: 3DMN (outboard canted branch)
branches.description: U28 (upstream undulator) → CUFE → outboard mirror MR-1 (34-ID-A) → masks (34-ID-B) → BPM, slits, small-offset HDCM with pink bypass, pink shutter (34-ID-C) → micro-diffraction instrument (≈60 m) and designed nano-diffraction position (≈65.5 m, installation unconfirmed) in 34-ID-E → pink beam stop at 66.9 m.

branches.name: ATOMIC (inboard, partner)
branches.description: Context only (ATOMIC has its own exhibit). Revolver U25/U21 (downstream undulator) → inboard mirror MR-2 → ATOMIC DCM and zoom KB1 in 34-ID-C → shielded pipe straight through 34-ID-E (55.1–67.5 m) → KB2 and coherent-imaging diffractometer in 34-ID-F (≈68–70 m) → beam stop 78.7 m.

components.name: 3DMN undulator (28 mm period, upstream)
components.distanceNote: Distances in this exhibit are measured, as in FDR Table 4.63, from the centre of the 34-ID straight (the canting-magnet position). The U28 is the upstream device; its centre is placed ≈1.2 m upstream (approximate: two 2.1 m devices plus a central canting magnet in the ≈4.8 m straight).
components.text: The X-ray source: a 2.1 m row of alternating permanent magnets with a 28 mm period, the repeat length of the magnet pattern, that steers the ring's 6 GeV electrons into a tight slalom, so they emit an intense, narrow X-ray beam. Closing the gap between the magnet rows strengthens the field and lowers the X-ray energies; at the 8.5 mm minimum gap its fundamental, the lowest of its emission peaks, lies near 3.0 keV, and higher energies come from odd harmonics, overtones at 3, 5, 7… times it. Laue diffraction wants a smooth spread of energies, so the gap can be tapered by up to 5 mm along the device to broaden the harmonics; whether this is used after the upgrade is not documented.

components.name: Canting magnets (0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad)
components.distanceNote: Centre magnet at the straight centre (0 m, the distance reference); 0.5 mrad magnets at both ends of the straight (≈±2.4 m, approx.).
components.text: Three small steering magnets kink the electron path by 1 mrad, about 0.06°, between the two undulators that share this straight section, so their X-ray beams drift apart and one slot in the ring feeds two beamlines: 3DMN and its neighbour ATOMIC. 3DMN takes the upstream undulator and the outboard beam, away from the ring; before the upgrade, its predecessor used the inboard one.

components.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator (U25/U21, downstream) – partner
components.distanceNote: Downstream device of the same straight, centre ≈+1.2 m from the straight centre (approx.).
components.text: The second undulator in the straight section feeds ATOMIC, the sister beamline next door, which images strain inside single nanocrystals with coherent X-rays. It is a 'revolver': two magnet rows, with 25 mm and 21 mm periods, share one support, and the device switches to whichever suits the chosen energy. It is shown for context and plays no part in 3DMN's experiments.

components.name: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE)
components.distanceNote: Front end occupies roughly 14–25 m inside the tunnel/ratchet wall; 19.4 m is the documented position of the upstream (GRID) mask. Other element positions not given in FDR – approximate.
components.text: The gatekeeper between accelerator and beamline, inside the tunnel's shielding. Its masks soak up kilowatts of unwanted heat (it is rated for two beams of 10 kW each), a fluorescence beam-position monitor measures where the beam points, and photon and safety shutters can stop it completely. It has no exit window: differential pumping keeps the vacuums apart, because a window there would degrade the beam's coherence.

specs.XBPM: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask
specs.elements: clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, burn-through fixed mask, GRID XBPM1, photon shutter 2, safety shutters

components.name: Front-end exit mask (two 2 × 2 mm² apertures)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A heavy metal block with two 2 mm square openings 1 mrad apart, one for each of the twin beams. It lets only the bright central core of each beam into the first optics hutch and absorbs the rest; a second beam-position monitor (XBPM2) is built into it.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A tungsten block with two 5 mm square openings, one per beam. It stops bremsstrahlung, very-high-energy gamma rays made when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring, from following the X-rays into the beamline. The openings were narrowed for the upgrade to help beamlines whose monochromators shift the beam only slightly, as 3DMN's does by about 1 mm.

components.name: White-beam slits, inboard (ATOMIC) 34ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: Adjustable jaws with tungsten edges that trim ATOMIC's beam while it still carries the undulator's full 'white' spectrum. They sit just upstream of 3DMN's own pair, each pair working on one of the twin beams.

components.name: White-beam slits, outboard (3DMN) 34ID-SL-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: Water-cooled jaws with tungsten edges that trim 3DMN's raw 'white' beam, which still carries the undulator's full spectrum and power, to the central millimetre or so its optics need. Removing the excess here keeps heat off the mirror: downstream, the mirror needs only about 1 × 1 mm of beam and the monochromator less than 0.3 × 0.3 mm.

specs.acceptance needed: ≈1 × 1 mm² at mirror, < 300 × 300 µm² at mono

components.name: Tungsten bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A tungsten shielding block with openings for the two X-ray beams. It stops stray gamma rays from the accelerator (bremsstrahlung) so that only the X-rays continue.

components.name: Lead bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-BC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A lead block just behind the tungsten collimator, adding a second layer of protection against stray high-energy radiation from the accelerator. Openings let the two X-ray beams through.

components.name: Outboard horizontal deflecting mirror 34ID-MR-1 (3DMN)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: 3DMN's first mirror: a flat, super-polished silicon mirror that the X-rays strike at a grazing 3 mrad (0.17°). It steers the 3DMN beam outboard, away from its twin, and acts as a filter: above a cutoff energy X-rays are no longer reflected, so the highest energies and much of the heat are left behind. Three coating stripes, bare silicon, rhodium and platinum, set estimated cutoffs near 10, 22 and 28 keV. A notch cut along the substrate reduces heat distortion about tenfold; the mirror absorbs up to 189 W.

specs.cooling: notch design (coolant not stated in FDR; PDR proposed LN₂)
specs.estimated cutoffs at 3 mrad: Si ≈10, Rh ≈22, Pt ≈28 keV (some usable flux to 30 keV, PDR)

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-SC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: Shielding just after the mirror. Once the X-ray beam has been bent, anything still travelling straight ahead, such as bremsstrahlung from the accelerator, is unwanted, and this collimator stops it.

components.name: Inboard horizontal deflecting mirror 34ID-MR-2 (ATOMIC)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: ATOMIC's twin of 3DMN's first mirror: flat silicon with silicon, rhodium and platinum stripes at the same 3 mrad grazing angle. It steers the neighbouring beam the other way, inboard toward the ring, so the two beams end up about 0.4 m apart in the 3DMN hutch.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-SC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (branch not stated).
components.text: Another collimator, stopping stray radiation that travels straight on past the second mirror. After the two mirrors, only the reflected beams should continue downstream.

components.name: Diagnostic flag 34ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A fluorescent screen that can drop into the beams and glow where the X-rays strike, so a camera shows staff exactly where both reflected beams are. It sits just after the two mirrors, before the beams leave the first optics hutch.

components.name: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop 34ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The end of the 'white' beam. A heavy block stops anything still travelling straight, while two openings pass the mirror-reflected beams, now called 'pink' because the mirrors have removed the highest energies. No white beam travels beyond this point.

components.name: Shielded transport A→B 34ID-ST-1
components.distanceNote: Spans 36.0–42.5 m (FDR Table 4.63; existing white-beam transport reused).
components.text: A lead-shielded vacuum pipe that carries both pink beams 6.5 m across the experiment-hall floor, from the first optics hutch to the next, so people can walk around it safely. It is the beamline's existing transport, reused.

components.name: Pink-beam photon mask, outboard 34ID-PM-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (inboard PM-2 at same position for ATOMIC).
components.text: A metal aperture that trims 3DMN's pink beam and protects everything downstream from a stray or misaligned beam. ATOMIC has a matching mask at the same position; the preliminary design described a septum mask here that splits the two beam paths into independent pipes.

components.name: Lead collimator / bremsstrahlung stop 34ID-BC-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The last heavy lead shielding against stray high-energy radiation before the optics hutch 34-ID-C. It also acts as a bremsstrahlung stop, absorbing gamma rays from the accelerator that would otherwise travel on with the X-rays.

components.name: ATOMIC double-crystal monochromator 34ID-MN-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (ATOMIC BPM 49.7 m and slits 50.3 m precede it).
components.text: ATOMIC's own monochromator, a near-twin of 3DMN's: two silicon crystals that pick out one X-ray energy between 5.3 and 30 keV, with a bypass for the full pink beam and a heated second crystal. ATOMIC uses the single-energy beam for coherent imaging. Shown for context.

components.name: ATOMIC zoom KB1 34ID-MR-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 gives 52.0 m; FDR text says 'station C at 54 m' – conflict noted.
components.text: The first of ATOMIC's two pairs of Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirrors, curved mirrors that focus X-rays at grazing incidence. They are bendable, and together with the second pair near ATOMIC's sample they zoom the spot between about 50 nm and 2 µm. Shown for context; its position is uncertain (52.0 m in a design table, 54 m in the text).

components.name: Beam position monitor, outboard 34ID-BD-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A beam-position monitor that measures exactly where 3DMN's pink beam is, just before its slits and monochromator. Pointing stability matters: any drift of the beam here shows up as motion of the 100 nm focus.

components.name: Slits (3D Nano) 34ID-SL-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: Precision jaws that choose how much of the beam travels on to the monochromator and the focusing mirrors. The preliminary design notes that the monochromator needs to accept less than 0.3 × 0.3 mm of beam.

components.name: Small-offset horizontal double-crystal monochromator 34ID-MN-2 (3DMN)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The monochromator: two silicon (111) crystals that reflect only the X-ray energy satisfying Bragg's law at their angle, selected to about one part in 10,000 over 5.3–30 keV. It is designed to slide out of the way in seconds, letting the full pink beam through (the mode shown here), and it reflects sideways, shifting the beam by only about 1.1 mm. To bring the single-energy beam back onto the pink one at the focus, the second crystal is kept about 60 °C warmer: the silicon expands, tilting the exit beam by an estimated 20–125 µrad depending on energy. Closing a full 1.1 mm offset at the micro mirrors would need about 180 µrad, so how the two beams are matched in practice awaits confirmation from the beamline staff.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter, outboard 34ID-SH-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (ATOMIC SH-1 at same position).
components.text: A heavy safety shutter for 3DMN's pink beam. When it closes, the 3DMN hutch 34-ID-E is safe to enter, even while ATOMIC's beam keeps running through it in its shielded pipe.

components.name: ATOMIC shielded transport through 34-ID-E 34ID-ST-2
components.distanceNote: Spans 55.1–67.5 m (FDR Table 4.63). In FDR Fig. 4.58 it runs ≈0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam (approx. from figure).
components.text: ATOMIC's beam passes straight through the 3DMN hutch inside a lead-shielded pipe 12.4 m long, about 0.4 m inboard of 3DMN's beam. People can enter 34-ID-E to work on 3DMN while ATOMIC runs next door.

components.name: Micro-focusing KB mirror pair (micro-diffraction instrument 34ID-BI-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 / text: KB and instrument at 60 m (ray traces at '60 m'). The pair deflects both vertically (first mirror) and horizontally (second mirror).
components.text: Two short curved mirrors, a Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) pair, focus the beam to about 100 nm: the first squeezes it vertically, the second horizontally, each at a grazing 3 mrad. Unlike lenses, mirrors bend every X-ray energy the same way, so the pink and single-energy beams share one focus. Ray tracing gives a design spot of 103 × 68 nm (horizontal × vertical, roughly full width at half maximum) at 14 keV, with 4.9 × 10¹² photons per second in a 0.1% energy band. To get there, the platinum-coated surfaces must match their ideal ellipses to within 0.5–0.75 nm (root-mean-square), a few atomic spacings. The beamline directory quotes 150 × 150 nm; no as-built measurement has been published.

components.name: Micro station sample stage (45° geometry)
components.distanceNote: Approx.: focus ≈0.1 m downstream of the 60.0 m KB position (PDR focal lengths f_v ≈142 mm, f_h ≈70 mm); not tabulated.
components.text: The sample sits tilted at 45° to the beam on a stack of motorised stages that step it through the focus in moves as small as about 10 nm, building a map point by point. An optical microscope looks squarely at its tilted face, and at least 50 mm between the last mirror and the focus leaves room for heaters, loading rigs and diamond-anvil pressure cells.

components.name: Depth-profiling wire / knife-edge scanner (DAXM)
components.distanceNote: Approx.: at the micro sample; wire ≈0.2–1 mm above the sample surface.
components.text: The depth finder: a platinum wire about 50–100 µm thick, roughly a hair's width, glides 0.2–1 mm above the sample surface in steps of about 1 µm. Each time its edge hides a diffraction spot, the straight line from that detector pixel past the wire's edge crosses the incoming beam at the depth where the spot was made: a moving shadow that pinpoints its source. A scan takes 50–2,000 frames per sample point and resolves 0.5–1 µm along the beam. The wire and its gap are enlarged in the model so they can be seen.

components.name: Coded aperture (gold barcode mask) – R&D option
components.distanceNote: Approx.: replaces the wire at the micro sample, ≈0.84–1 mm above the surface (as in the 34-ID-E tests); drawn parked beside the wire.
components.text: An experimental alternative to the wire: a gold 'barcode' on a thin silicon nitride membrane, a 256-bit pattern of bars and gaps in which no run of 8 bits repeats. One short sweep of about 120 µm encodes the depth of every spot at once, so a 3D scan needs about a fifth of the frames a wire would. The gold is about 4.6 µm thick, with nominal 7.5 µm bars and 15 µm gaps. Shown parked beside the wire, enlarged.

specs.as fabricated: Au bars ≈4.5 µm wider than nominal

components.name: Main area detector above the sample (90° reflection geometry)
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position = micro sample (60.1 m). Panel centre ≈0.513 m above the sample and ≈30 mm downstream of it, face horizontal (pre-upgrade lauelab geometry file geoN_2023-04-06; 510.9 mm in Gursoy et al. 2022).
components.text: A large flat X-ray camera hangs about half a metre above the sample, looking down, and catches the Laue spots thrown up at around 90°, a fingerprint of each grain's tilt and strain. Before the upgrade it was a PerkinElmer amorphous-silicon panel with 2048 × 2048 pixels of 200 µm; at that distance one pixel corresponds to about 2 × 10⁻⁴ in lattice spacing, so the quoted 10⁻⁴ precision relies on locating spots to a fraction of a pixel. The design called for a low-noise photon-counting detector of the Pilatus 6M class, but its purchase was cut from the project; the detector in use now is not documented. The coloured rays in the model are calculated for two nickel grains, coloured by each spot's X-ray energy.

components.name: Two side area detectors
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position ≈ micro sample; panel centres ≈0.14 m upstream of it. Each panel is tilted 45° about the beam axis (face normal pointing up-and-outboard / up-and-inboard), ≈0.40 m perpendicular distance, centre ≈0.43 m from the sample: 'Yellow' outboard, 'Purple' inboard (pre-upgrade lauelab geometry file geoN_2023-04-06).
components.text: Two smaller cameras, tilted in from either side about 0.4 m from the sample, catch spots the main camera misses. A wider spread of spots pins down each grain's orientation and distortion more precisely, especially the shear components of strain. Before the upgrade they were PerkinElmer panels of 1024 × 1024 pixels, nicknamed 'Yellow' (outboard) and 'Purple' (inboard); the design calls for 1–2 megapixel detectors.

components.name: Fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position ≈ micro sample; snout a few cm from the sample (approx.).
components.text: Atoms struck by the beam emit X-rays at energies unique to each element. This silicon drift detector, its snout a few centimetres from the sample, reads that fluorescence to map the chemistry and to find landmarks on the sample. The preliminary design preferred a 1 mm thick sensor to catch higher-energy emission lines.

components.name: Far-field coherent (BCDI) detector, movable
components.distanceNote: Approx.: PDR places it ≈2–3 m from the micro sample (e.g. 3.3 m at 12 keV for 1.5 µm particles with 75 µm pixels). Drawn ≈2.2 m away, up and outboard (2θ ≈72°, e.g. Ni 400 at 12 keV) so the diffracted ray leaves through the 45° sample surface and clears the gantry and side detectors; its along-beam coordinate is therefore ≈60.8 m. Position illustrative.
components.text: A camera on a robot or large translation stage, about 2–3 m away, records the fine speckle around a single diffraction spot. A computer turns that speckle into a 3D image of one grain's shape and internal strain (Bragg coherent diffraction imaging), made practical by the upgraded source's coherence. Energy scans step through the reflection while the sample stays fixed. Micro station only; its position in the model is illustrative.

components.name: Nano-diffraction thermal enclosure
components.distanceNote: Approx.: upstream wall of a ≈2.8–3 m enclosure around the 65.5 m instrument (3000 mm dimension in FDR Fig. 4.67; ≈2.5 m footprint at ≈64.3–66.8 m in Fig. 4.58).
components.text: The nano station is designed to sit in its own clear-walled room, about 3 m long, inside the hutch. A 10 cm aluminium part grows by 100 nm, more than twice the 40 nm design spot, if it warms by just 0.04 °C, so this enclosure is meant to hold the air steady to 0.02 °C; the hutch itself is held to 0.03–0.05 °C. The design also moves the electronics outside and stands the instrument on an ultra-stable table, because the old steel-legged table vibrated by about 50 nm.

components.name: Nano-focusing KB mirror pair (nano-diffraction instrument 34ID-BI-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 / text: 65.5 m (ray traces at '65 m'). The pair deflects both vertically (first mirror) and horizontally (second mirror).
components.text: A shorter-focus Kirkpatrick–Baez mirror pair, further from the source at 65.5 m, designed to squeeze the beam to about 40 nm: 37 × 37 nm at 14 keV in ray-traced design, with 4.9 × 10¹¹ photons per second in a 0.1% energy band, ten times less than the micro station. Its platinum-coated surfaces must be accurate to 0.4–0.5 nm (root-mean-square), and the working distance shrinks to about 30 mm. Whether the nano station has been installed and commissioned is not publicly documented as of October 2026.

components.name: Nano station sample stage with interferometric nanopositioners
components.distanceNote: Approx.: a few cm downstream of the nano KB.
components.text: An ultra-precise stage, tracked by laser interferometers, holds the sample steady to a few nanometres (about 5 nm in the preliminary design) while it is scanned through the 40 nm spot. It rests on an ultra-stable optical table inside the thermal enclosure.

components.name: Nano station precision knife-edge / wire scanner
components.distanceNote: Approx.: just above the sample.
components.text: The nano station's depth finder: a precision knife edge or wire, moved with about 5 nm precision just above the sample. It uses the same moving-shadow principle as the micro station's wire and coded aperture, at a finer scale.

components.name: Nano station flat-panel detectors
components.distanceNote: Above/around the sample (approx.).
components.text: Flat X-ray cameras above and beside the nano sample collect its Laue patterns. The volume the beam probes is tiny, and the diffracted signal shrinks with the thickness of each depth slice, so these detectors must be very low-noise. The design calls for one large detector above, two at the sides and one for forward scattering; what is installed is unknown.

components.name: Pink-beam stop, outboard 34ID-BS-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63; end of the 3DMN beam.
components.text: The end of the line for 3DMN: a block of heavy metal at 66.9 m, by the wall between hutches E and F, that safely absorbs whatever remains of the pink beam. ATOMIC's beam continues past it in its shielded pipe.

components.name: ATOMIC coherent-imaging endstation (34ID-BI-3) – partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (KB2 at 68.1 m; beam stop 78.7 m).
components.text: Next door in 34-ID-F, ATOMIC uses the twin beam for coherent imaging of strain inside individual nanocrystals, with sample and detector diffractometers. A design table places its second zoom mirror pair at 68.1 m; the drawings put it closer to the sample, and the as-built position is unpublished. It works over the same 5.3–30 keV range. Listed here for context only.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-A
enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (FOE), white beam; shared by 3DMN and ATOMIC
enclosures.notes: Boundaries read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (about ±0.3 m; width very approximate). Contains FE exit mask/collimator, both CUFE white-beam slits, W and Pb collimators, both horizontal deflecting mirrors (29.6 m, 31.3 m), secondary collimators, diagnostic flag and the pink mask / white-beam stop (34.0 m). Downstream of PM-1 only pink beam exists.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-B
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58. Reached via shielded transport 36.0–42.5 m. Houses inboard/outboard pink photon masks (46.9 m) and Pb collimator/bremsstrahlung stop (47.3 m).

enclosures.name: 34-ID-C
enclosures.role: Optics enclosure for both branches (repurposed former 34-ID-C coherent-diffraction station)
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58. ATOMIC BPM/slits/DCM/KB1 (49.7–52.0 m), 3DMN BPM (52.7), slits (53.1), HDCM (53.8) and both pink-beam shutters (54.8 m) at its downstream wall. Downstream wall placed at ≈55.0 m: FDR Table 4.63 puts the pink-beam shutters (inside C) at 54.8 m and the start of the 'shielded pipe through 34-ID-E' at 55.1 m.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-E
enclosures.role: 3DMN experimental station (micro- and nano-diffraction instruments); ATOMIC transport passes through
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58/4.68: stepped outline, ≈2.6 m wide from ≈55.0 to ≈59.3 m (footprint of the old 34-ID-D third optics enclosure) and ≈4.3 m wide from ≈59.3 to 67.5 m. PDR (2017) planned to join the old D and E stations and add ≈2 m. Instrument footprints drawn at ≈58.2–60.7 m (micro) and ≈64.3–66.8 m (nano). Requires 0.03–0.05 °C air stability and a temperature-stabilized user/control area at the entrance (PDR). Upstream wall ≈55.0 m constrained by FDR Table 4.63 (shutters 54.8 m in C; ST-2 'through 34-ID-E' 55.1–67.5 m). The FDR's instrument ESD is titled '34-ID-D/E 3DMN Endstation Instrumentation', consistent with D and E having been merged.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-F
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58; trapezoidal hutch with a large detector arm; ATOMIC beam stop at 78.7 m.

instruments.name: 3D micro-diffraction instrument (34ID-BI-1)
instruments.text: The workhorse station, at about 60 m. A Kirkpatrick–Baez mirror pair, two curved mirrors focusing in turn vertically and horizontally, brings pink (multi-energy) or single-energy X-rays to about 100 nm (103 × 68 nm in design at 14 keV; the directory quotes 150 × 150 nm) on a sample tilted at 45°. A wire or gold coded aperture sweeps above it for depth, area detectors above and beside it catch the Laue spots, and a far detector can record coherent speckle for Bragg coherent imaging. Each map point takes a scan of 50–2,000 frames, which software reconstructs into depth, indexes and turns into orientation and strain; energy scans add absolute strain. At least 50 mm between mirror and focus leaves room for heaters, loading rigs, diamond-anvil cells and an in situ nanoindenter.
detectors: Large area detector above the sample in 90° reflection geometry (pre-upgrade PerkinElmer XRD1621, 2048 × 2048, at ≈511 mm; design Pilatus 6M class).
Two side area detectors (pre-upgrade PerkinElmer 1024 × 1024 panels, XRD 0820 AN / 'PE0822'; design 1–2 Mpixel).
Forward-scattering medium area detector on a horizontal motion (PDR); the pre-upgrade directory lists a Mar 165 CCD for forward scattering.
Movable far-field small-pixel detector at ≈2–3 m for Bragg coherent imaging.
Ion chambers before and after the KB mirrors (pre-upgrade I_start, I_middle, I_final).
sampleEnvironments: Small environmental chambers within the ≥ 50 mm working distance (PDR).
Heating and cooling, electric and magnetic fields, and mechanical loading (FDR science scope).

instruments.name: 3D nano-diffraction instrument (34ID-BI-2)
instruments.text: A quieter twin at the back of the hutch, at 65.5 m, designed to focus to about 40 nm for the finest details. It is meant to sit in its own clear-walled enclosure held steady to 0.02 °C, on an ultra-stable table, with interferometer-tracked stages accurate to about 5 nm and very low-noise detectors, since each thin depth slice gives only a faint signal. Its shorter working distance, about 30 mm, limits it to compact sample environments. Whether it has been built and commissioned is not publicly documented as of October 2026.
detectors: Flat-panel or photon-counting area detectors above and beside the sample (design).
sampleEnvironments: The reduced working distance (≈30 mm, PDR) limits environments to compact stages.

geometryNotes:
The beamlines form a canted pair: 3DMN takes the upstream undulator of the 34-ID straight and the outboard beam; ATOMIC takes the downstream undulator and the inboard beam, 1 mrad apart (FDR). This reverses the pre-upgrade assignment (the old 34-ID-E used the inboard beam).

Each branch has its own flat mirror in 34-ID-A at 3.0 mrad grazing incidence (6 mrad deflection): 3DMN at 29.6 m, ATOMIC at 31.3 m. The PDR states that the 3DMN mirror deflects outboard and ATOMIC's inboard (≈11 mrad between the pink beams at 2.5 mrad), and the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic shows the same; in FDR Fig. 4.58 the 3DMN pink beam runs ≈0.4 m outboard of the ATOMIC shielded pipe through 34-ID-E (read from the drawing; consistent with opposite deflections: ≈58 mm from canting plus ≈6 mrad × 28 m on each side). Both monochromators are horizontally deflecting small-offset (≈1.1 mm) DCMs in 34-ID-C, so the monochromatic beam is offset sideways by ≈1 mm, not upward.

All hutches are on the experiment floor within the existing sector-34 footprint (no long-beamline building): A (FOE) ≈24.4–36.0 m, shielded transport 36.0–42.5 m, B ≈42.3–47.8 m, C ≈47.8–55.0 m, E ≈55.0–67.5 m (stepped width), F ≈67.5–79.8 m (read from the FDR figure scale bar).

Inside E the 3DMN beam ends at a pink-beam stop at 66.9 m, while ATOMIC's beam continues in a shielded pipe (55.1–67.5 m) into F.

Instrument geometry: beam along +Z; sample surface tilted 45° (normal pointing up and upstream); the main detector looks straight down on the sample from ≈0.5 m above (2θ ≈ 90° at its centre); two side detectors at ≈0.4 m perpendicular distance (≈0.43 m to their centres), outboard and inboard, slightly upstream and raised; the wire moves along H = (Y+Z)/√2, parallel to the sample surface, ≈0.2–1 mm above it; the KB pair sits just upstream of the sample (vertical mirror first, horizontal mirror ≈6–7 cm from the focus at the micro station, per the PDR focal lengths).

34-ID-E coordinates: X horizontal outboard (toward the hutch doors), Y up, Z downstream. The nano instrument sits inside a ≈3 m long glass thermal enclosure on an ultra-stable table at the downstream end of E.

Exhibit conventions: distances are measured from the centre of the 34-ID straight (U28 centre at ≈−1.2 m, ATOMIC revolver at ≈+1.2 m); hutch outlines and offsets are read from FDR Fig. 4.58; the 1 mrad canting plus opposite 6 mrad mirror deflections put the two beams ≈0.4 m apart in 34-ID-E. Sub-millimetre parts (wire, coded aperture, sample gap, DCM crystal offset) are enlarged in the 3D model for visibility; their true sizes are given in the text.

interactiveIdeas.title: Laue constellation: rainbow vs. one colour
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitor rotates a crystal (e.g. fcc Ni) under a focused beam. Pink mode: a constellation of spots appears on a detector panel 0.5 m above. Mono mode: almost all spots vanish; an energy slider scans until one spot lights up, revealing its exact energy.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why polychromatic Laue sees every grain without rotating the sample, why spot positions give orientation, and why a single-colour energy scan is needed to get the absolute lattice spacing.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg: λ = 2 d sin(θ); E[keV] = 12.398/λ[Å]. k_out = k_in - 2(k_in·n)n for plane normal n; a spot exists if the required energy E_hkl = 12.398/(2 d_hkl sin θ) lies in the incident band (~5-30 keV after the mirror; most signal 12-17 keV on the top detector). Harmonics (nh nk nl) land on the same pixel. Top detector centre at 2θ = 90°, so E = 12.398/(√2 d). Spot intensity ~ |F_hkl|² × spectrum × Lorentz/polarization; undulator harmonics (U28 E1 = 12.2/(1+K²/2) keV) make the 'rainbow' lumpy unless tapered.

interactiveIdeas.title: The wire that sees depth (DAXM)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Side view: beam enters a 45° sample; three grains at different depths send rays up to a pixelated detector. Visitor drags a wire across; per-pixel intensity curves step down; taking the difference and tracing the ray past the wire edge places each signal at its depth, building a 3D grain map.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Depth resolution comes from geometry (pinhole-camera triangulation), not from focusing; why many frames are needed and what limits resolution.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Depth along beam D = intersection of the line (pixel → tangent point on wire edge) with the beam line (lauelab formulas: tan(φ) = (tan φ0 ∓ tan dφ)/(1 ± tan φ0 tan dφ), tan dφ = a/√(r² - a²)). For a pixel directly above the wire, a wire step dH along H = (Y+Z)/√2 moves the triangulated point along the beam by dH/√2 × L/(L-h) ~ 0.71 dH (h = wire height ~0.2-1 mm, L ~ 510 mm). Pixel blur ~ p·h/L ~ 0.08-0.4 µm for 200 µm pixels. Depth below surface = depth along beam × sin(45°). Leading edge removes intensity (positive difference), trailing edge restores it (negative). Wire diameter 50-100 µm Pt; step ~1 µm; scan length set by the angular fan (hundreds of µm).

interactiveIdeas.title: Barcode for X-rays (coded aperture)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Replace the wire with a gold barcode built from a de Bruijn sequence. Each pixel records an on/off 'Morse code'; the visitor slides a window along the code to find the unique match and thus the depth. A race: wire scan vs. barcode scan to reconstruct the same grain map.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How x-ray-astronomy coded apertures were miniaturised to speed up 3D microscopy; uniqueness of every 8-bit window; trade-off between bit size, thickness and noise.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Order-8 binary de Bruijn sequence, length 256 (every 8-bit substring unique); bits 7.5 µm (Au, 1) / 15 µm (open, 0) → ≥ 120 µm scan for unique decoding vs ~600 µm wire scan; measurement d = A_p s (Toeplitz coding matrix); decode by exhaustive offset search + NNLS; 4.6 µm Au transmits a significant fraction at 20-30 keV (contrast drops with energy and with obliquity up to ~20° on a 51 cm detector); signals larger than a bit blur the code.

interactiveIdeas.title: Shrink the source, shrink the spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Split screen: old APS vs APS-U source shapes (280 × 10 µm vs 14.7 × 3.2 µm rms) feed the same KB pair. Sliders for mirror distance/focal length, slit opening and mirror figure error show spot size and flux.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: A focused spot is an image of the source; brightness, not just flux, sets how small and intense the spot can be; why the old station had to throw away photons with slits and why sub-nanometre mirror figure is needed.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot FWHM ~ √[(2.355 σ_src q/p)² + (diffraction ~ 0.88 λ q / D, D = illuminated mirror aperture, i.e. 0.44 λ/NA with NA = D/2q)² + (~2 × 2.355 × σ_slope × q)²]; demagnification p/q ~ 60 m / 0.07-0.15 m ~ 400-900; source FWHM = 2.355 σ (horizontal 35 µm APS-U vs 660 µm old). Use FDR results as anchors: 103 × 68 nm² (micro), 37 × 37 nm² (nano) at 14 keV (FWHM-like; RMS ~50 × 35 and ~19 × 19 nm, FDR Figs. 4.60-4.61); tolerance 0.4-0.75 nm rms figure error for <10% growth. Beam pointing: a lateral source shift dx moves the focus by dx q/p; an angular error dψ of the beam at the KB moves it by ~dψ × q.

interactiveIdeas.title: Flip the monochromator, keep the spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Animated small-offset DCM: crystals slide in (single colour) and out (pink). A heater on crystal 2 slowly warms it; the exit beam tilts until the mono spot overlaps the pink spot on the sample.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How thermal expansion of silicon is used as a micro-steering knob; why pink and mono must hit the same sub-micron volume.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Si(111) d = 3.1356 Å; θ_B from 21.9° (5.3 keV) to 3.8° (30 keV). Heating crystal 2 by ΔT changes d by α ΔT (α_Si ~ 2.6 × 10⁻⁶ /K); Bragg angle mismatch Δθ = α ΔT tan(θ_B); exit-beam tilt 2 Δθ (~125 / 70 / 45 / 21 µrad at 5.3 / 9 / 14 / 30 keV for 60 K). Offset ~1.1 mm; closing it at the micro KB ~6 m downstream would need ~180 µrad, at the nano KB ~11.7 m downstream ~95 µrad. Horizontal-deflection polarization loss: PDR kinematic cos²(2θ) estimate ~1/2 at 5.3 keV, ~1/4 at 8 keV, ~10% at 12 keV; perfect-crystal (Darwin-width) scaling |cos 2θ| gives ~28% / ~12% / ~5%. dE/E ~ 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ for Si(111). Present the FDR wording ('intersects the pink beam at the sample') and flag the exact criterion as unconfirmed.

interactiveIdeas.title: Strain decoder: what moves a Laue spot?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Apply a rotation, a shear (deviatoric) strain, or a uniform expansion to a crystal and watch the Laue spots. Rotation moves all spots together; shear changes angles between spots; uniform expansion moves nothing - until you switch to the monochromator and see the energy shift.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Laue patterns measure orientation and 5 of the 6 strain components; the 6th (volume change) needs one energy measurement; how this maps dislocation cells and residual stress in printed metals.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot directions depend only on q-hat = q/|q|; a uniform dilatation scales all |q| without changing directions (invisible to Laue). Deviatoric strain ~10⁻⁴ resolution (best ~2 × 10⁻⁵). One 200 µm pixel at 510 mm is ~3.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad in 2θ, i.e. ~2 × 10⁻⁴ rad in the plane-normal direction (~2 × 10⁻⁴ in dd/d at 2θ = 90°); sub-pixel peak fitting over many reflections reaches 10⁻⁴ or better (the PDR's design rule of '1 pixel ~ 10⁻⁴' is a goal, not met exactly at 0.51 m). Rotations of 0.01° are easily visible. Full tensor = deviatoric (Laue) + dilatational (one reflection's energy, dE/E ~10⁻⁴).

funFacts: The 3DMN nano-focusing mirrors must match their ideal elliptical shape to within 0.4–0.5 nanometres rms – only a couple of atomic spacings – or the 40 nm spot blurs (FDR 2019).
A 10-cm piece of aluminium grows by 100 nm if it warms by just 0.04 °C, so the nano station sits in its own enclosure held to 0.02 °C (PDR 2017).

Using a sliding wire as a 'differential aperture' to get depth from a Laue pattern was introduced by the ORNL team of Larson, Yang, Ice, Budai and Tischler at the APS and published in Nature in 2002; it became the signature technique of 34-ID-E.

The old station's depth wire was a ≈50 micrometre platinum wire hovering ≈200 micrometres above the sample (34-ID-E 'End near focus' photo of the CCD-era, pre-2009 setup); 2022–23 geometry files use a 101.5 µm wire.
The gold 'barcode' coded aperture uses a de Bruijn sequence: in its 256 bits, every run of 8 bits appears exactly once – an idea borrowed from X-ray astronomy (Gursoy et al. 2022).

In 3DMN's monochromator the second silicon crystal is kept about 60 °C warmer than the first; silicon's thermal expansion then tilts the exit beam by roughly 0.02–0.13 milliradian (more at low energies), intended to bring the single-colour and rainbow beams onto the same path (FDR); how the as-built system keeps both on the same sub-100 nm spot is unpublished.

Most of the Laue signal on the top detector comes from photons of about 12–17 keV: at lower energies few sets of atomic planes can reflect to 90 degrees, and at higher energies the reflections grow weak (PDR).
Before the upgrade, demand was so high that 34-ID-E proposals typically needed a review score of about 1.4 – closer to 'extraordinary' than 'excellent' – to get beam time (PDR).
As early as 2005, 34-ID-E demonstrated achromatic mirror focusing to 85 × 95 nm² at 15 keV (APS User Meeting poster, Liu et al.).
The design team estimated the upgrade could make some 3D experiments up to 45,000 times faster: ×100 brighter source, ×9 better mirrors, ×5 coded apertures, ×10 better detectors (PDR).
3DMN is expected to produce ≈2.8 petabytes of raw data a year, about 7 times the pre-upgrade station (APS computing strategy 2024).
ATOMIC's X-ray beam travels straight through the 3DMN hutch inside a shielded pipe, so both beamlines can run while people work in 34-ID-E (FDR).
Before the upgrade 3DMN's predecessor used the inboard canted beam; after the upgrade 3DMN takes the outboard one (34-ID-E wiki vs FDR Table 4.62 / Fig. 4.59).

A 2026 study fed 3D wire-scan maps of a stainless-steel grain from 34-ID-E to an unsupervised machine-learning model to pick out dislocation cells at 0.5 micrometre depth resolution (SharafEldin et al.).

openQuestions: Nano-diffraction station: FDR (2019) specifies it at 65.5 m, but no public 2024–2026 source confirms it is installed/commissioned; the 2024 APS computing strategy says the APS-U project 'descoped certain parts of the 3DMN Feature beamline, including detector purchases', and APS updates describe only 'infrastructure' for 34-ID being delivered within the project. Treat the nano station as designed, status unknown. A Dec 2021 user town hall covered 'timing and scope of the 34-ID construction' but its slides are not public.

As-built detectors: unknown. Pre-upgrade 34-ID-E used PerkinElmer XRD1621 (top) + 2× XRD0820 (sides); the design called for Pilatus-6M-class + two 1–2M detectors; purchases were descoped from APS-U. ATOMIC's directory lists an Eiger 500K 'for Laue diffraction only' at 34-ID-F – not evidence for 3DMN. Aug 2026: the coded-aperture team's ModSim talk says a new detector with ≈10× collection speed is planned and lists 'Wire Reconstructions (HPC possible with Eiger)' – which detector is installed now is still not stated publicly.

As-built focal sizes/flux: FDR ray traces give 103 × 68 nm² (micro) and 37 × 37 nm² (nano) at 14 keV; the Beamline Directory quotes 0.15 × 0.15 µm and 10¹⁴ (pink) / 10¹¹ (mono, 15 keV) ph/s; no commissioning measurement has been published. MEDSI 2025 states all feature beamlines met their KPPs but gives no 3DMN numbers. Note that APS-U feature-beamline KPPs were brightness at a defined energy and usable energy range (only ISN had a spot-size KPP), so meeting the KPP does not certify the 3DMN focal size.
Undulator length: FDR gives 2.1 m for both canted devices; the ATOMIC directory entry says its revolver is 2.3 m. As-built 3DMN U28 length not independently confirmed.

First-mirror cooling: PDR (2017) proposed LN₂-cooled Si mirrors; FDR (2019) specifies flat 3-stripe Si mirrors at 3.0 mrad with a 'notch' anti-deformation design but no coolant. Deflection sense is no longer open in the design record: the PDR text and the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic both show 3DMN deflecting outboard and ATOMIC inboard, consistent with the ≈0.4 m separation in Fig. 4.58; as-built confirmation still welcome.

Mono heater criterion: the FDR says the heated second crystal tilts the mono beam so it 'intersects the pink beam at the sample position'; Pateras et al. (34-ID-C precursor) say it keeps the mono beam 'coincident to the pink beam in the final focusing optics' – these describe the same crossing point (KB ≈0.1 m from the sample), so they do not conflict. The open issue is quantitative: 2·α·ΔT·tan(θ_B) at ΔT ≈ 60 K gives ≈20–125 µrad (30 → 5.3 keV), whereas closing a 1.1 mm offset at the micro KB (≈6 m) needs ≈180 µrad and at the nano KB (≈11.7 m) ≈95 µrad; and a crossing angle ψ at the KB shifts the focus by ≈ψ × q (microns). How the as-built system keeps pink and mono on the same sub-100 nm spot (energy-dependent ΔT, KB re-alignment, residual offset) needs confirmation from beamline staff.

Hutch boundaries and widths are read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (about ±0.3 m; widths rougher); 34-ID-D no longer appears in the FDR naming and appears to have been absorbed into the enlarged 34-ID-E.

Sample positions: FDR tabulates instrument/KB positions (60.0 m, 65.5 m); actual focal-plane positions depend on as-built focal lengths (PDR design 70/142 mm micro, 55/120 mm nano, working distance ≥ 50 / ≈30 mm).

Depth-resolution hardware in routine use after the upgrade (Pt wire vs coded aperture/mask scans): coded apertures are demonstrated (2022–2025) and 'mask scan' reconstruction was 'R&D prototyping' in 2024; routine user availability not confirmed.
Whether undulator gap taper (supported up to 5 mm by the APS-U HPMU drive) is used to smooth the pink-beam spectrum for Laue after the upgrade.
Energy range: 5.3–30 keV (FDR, PDR) vs 5.5–30 keV (current directory).

Status: on 2026-10-05 3DMN was at stage 5 (scientific commissioning/early experiments); the date it enters the general user program (stage 6) is not announced, although 34-ID-E already appears on the GU proposal beamline list. Early 2D experiments ran around late July 2026 and 3D (HPC-scale coded-aperture) experiments were planned 'in winter' (ModSim 2026 talk).

Minor FDR inconsistency for the partner beamline: ATOMIC KB1 at 52.0 m (Table 4.63) vs 'station C at 54 m' (text). Also the old 34-ID-E wiki says the canted beams are separated by '1 µrad' – an obvious typo for 1 mrad.

Pink-beam flux comparison: PDR says ≈10¹⁴ ph/s pink is '≈50×' current operations at 500 nm, while the 2016 web spec lists 10¹¹ ph/s (white) for the old station – the two pre-upgrade baselines are inconsistent.

Detector model naming: the pre-upgrade top panel is 'XRD 1621' in Das et al. 2018 and the lauelab geometry ID ('PE1621'), but 'XRD 1620 AN' in the 2024 computing strategy; the side panels are 'XRD 0820 AN' on the Instruments page/computing strategy but 'PE0822' in 2022–23 geometry files. The generic name 'PerkinElmer 2k × 2k / 1k × 1k a-Si flat panels' avoids implying that the model assignment is confirmed.
